title: How 500 Men Toppled an Empire
description: Five hundred Spaniards did not conquer millions of people with guns. Disease, Native allies, and empires already cracking did the real work — in Mexico and in Peru.
essential_question: Why did guns alone not account for the Spanish victories?
learning_objectives: Explain why Spanish weapons alone cannot account for the fall of Tenochtitlan.
Describe how smallpox and the Tlaxcalan alliance decided the conquest of Mexico.
Compare the falls of the Mexica and Inca empires as one repeating pattern.

key_terms.definition: A Spanish conqueror in the Americas, e.g. Cortés in Mexico and Pizarro in Peru.
The Mexica capital, taken by Cortés and his Tlaxcalan allies in 1521.
The Mexica's rival whose tens of thousands of warriors formed Cortés's real army.
Sahagún's multivolume history compiled with Nahua collaborators; Book 12 records the 1520 smallpox epidemic.
Where Pizarro's 168 men seized the Inca emperor Atahualpa, then ransomed and executed him.
The war between Huáscar and Atahualpa after Huayna Capac's death that left the Inca Empire fractured.

narration.text: [solemn]In [date:1519], [es]Hernán Cortés[/es], a conquistador, a Spanish conqueror, landed on the coast of Mexico with five hundred soldiers. Sixteen horses. Fourteen cannons. The [es]Mexica[/es] Empire ruled millions of people from [es]Tenochtitlan[/es], a city larger than London. [beat] Two years later, the empire was gone. Five hundred men did that. How?

narration.text: [VOICE:cortes][fierce]They had never seen a horse. Never heard a gun. We were few, but we were thunder. [VOICE:host]So guns win? [beat] Not so fast. [es]Cortés[/es] had fourteen cannons. Fourteen. They took a minute to reload. And the [es]Mexica[/es] adapted. They stopped meeting the cavalry in open fields and fought where horses couldn't go. The weapons helped. But fourteen cannons don't topple an empire.

narration.text: [solemn]Here's what the cannons can't explain. In the fall of [date:1520], smallpox tore through [es]Tenochtitlan[/es]. It killed the emperor [es]Cuitláhuac[/es] after eighty days on the throne. It killed warriors, priests, leaders, everyone who could organize a defense. [beat] A Franciscan friar named [es]Sahagún[/es] spent decades interviewing [es]Mexica[/es] survivors. He asked the survivors what the sickness was like. One of them told him.

narration.text: [beat] [es]Cortés[/es] already knew the trick. Before the plague, before the siege, he'd walked into [es]Tenochtitlan[/es] and seized [es]Moctezuma[/es] himself, holding the emperor hostage for months. And he didn't come back alone. The [es]Tlaxcalans[/es], the [es]Mexica[/es]'s oldest enemies, gave him tens of thousands of warriors. Why fight for the strangers? The [es]Mexica[/es] had spent generations raiding [es]Tlaxcala[/es] for tribute and captives for sacrifice, the Flower Wars. The [es]Tlaxcalans[/es] didn't join [es]Cortés[/es]. They used him. At the final siege, the Spanish gave the orders. The [es]Tlaxcalans[/es] did the fighting and took most of the casualties.

narration.text: In Peru, eleven years later, [es]Francisco Pizarro[/es] ran the same play on an empire already broken. Smallpox had killed the Inca emperor [es]Huayna Capac[/es] around [date:1527], years before [es]Pizarro[/es] arrived. The disease outran him. [es]Huayna Capac[/es]'s sons, [es]Huáscar[/es] and [es]Atahualpa[/es], then fought a brutal war of succession, brother against brother. [es]Atahualpa[/es] won, but the empire was bleeding when [es]Pizarro[/es] walked in. [beat] At [es]Cajamarca[/es], in [date:1532], [es]Pizarro[/es]'s hundred and sixty-eight men seized the emperor [es]Atahualpa[/es] in the town square.

narration.text: So here's the playbook. Turn the empire's enemies into your army. Cut off the head. Let disease do the rest. [beat] Guns helped, but they were the smallest part of the answer. [2s pause] So who conquered Mexico? [es]Cortés[/es] gave the orders. [2s pause] Everyone else did the conquering.
